 · Speaking the truth scores higher than writing beautifully.  We verify each statement in the report against the code and proactively write "this was not done" and "this number is an estimated value" for the team, and the completeness is higher.

import subprocess, json, collections, sys

R = r"D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge"
BR = "openvela/dev-ai-contest-2026"

def git(*args):
    return subprocess.run(["git", "-C", R] + list(args),
                          capture_output=True, check=True)

paths = [p for p in git("ls-tree", "-r", "--name-only", BR, "--", "logs"
                        ).stdout.decode("utf-8").splitlines() if p.endswith(".jsonl")]

roles = collections.Counter()
days = set()
total_lines = 0
total_bytes = 0
dates = []

for p in paths:
    blob = git("show", "%s:%s" % (BR, p)).stdout
    total_bytes += len(blob)
    days.add(p.split("/")[2])
    for line in blob.splitlines():
        if not line.strip():

        try:
            ev = json.loads(line.decode("utf-8"))

        roles[ev.get("role", "?")] += 1

print()

**1. What I didn't build — and the one gap I did.**
LVGL, the NuttX audio stack with the ES8311 codec, the `apps/video` camera stack for the OV5640, TFLite-Micro, littlefs, USB CDC-NCM networking, and the `ai_agent` framework all came with the OS. What was missing was INT8 kernels for the Xtensa LX7 — so I ported them. Single inference went from **6.75 s to 1.31 s**. **2. POSIX compatibility isn't a checkbox — it changed how I debugged.**
My agent call froze the entire chip. I found it with `cat /proc/<pid>/stack` — a Linux debugging workflow, on an MCU. The cause: a pthread stack had been allocated in PSRAM, and a littlefs flash read disables the cache that PSRAM is reached through. Three Kconfig symbols fixed it. On a traditional RTOS I'd have been reading a linker map and guessing.

**3. The AI layer is the part I could not have done on a traditional RTOS.**
`ai_agent` shipped with the tool registry, Skills and LLM transport. One ~40-line Markdown Skill file, and the feeder proactively reports each pet's appetite. But the integration was the real work: my request body was **19,391 bytes against a 12,544-byte IOB pool**. Cutting 20 unused tools took end-to-end latency from **150–300 s down to 3.6–35.6 s**. text:
I checked every claim in the draft against the submitted English report on `dev-ai-contest-2026`. Three things in the draft didn't match, and I've fixed them.

## What changed

| Draft said | The report says | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| ESP-NN is something I "could contribute back into the tree" | L693: ESP-NN is **not included in the team repo**. It was submitted as a fork/PR, so the repo runs the slower 6.75 s kernels out of the box. | Say it's "submitted as a fork/PR". Don't imply it's merged. |
| The Skill is a "~40-line" file | The file is **26 lines** (185 words). | Say "26 lines". |
| Found by reading `/proc/<pid>/stack` | The report never mentions this. | Removed. |

Two other notes:
- **POSIX:** the report never uses the word "POSIX", so I don't make that claim. Point 2 uses the reuse list from the report's table (L284–289) instead.
- **Heap size:** the shipped value is **0x48000** (L290/L490). Your early fix note had 0x30000, but L490 says 0x30000 stops the freeze and still can't ship. Don't quote 0x30000.

Everything else checks out: 6.75 s → 1.31 s, CONV_2D at 84%, "cmsis-nn and nnlib-hifi4 only, nothing for LX7", the 19,391 B request with 9,946 B of tool schema, the 12,544 B buffer pool (~7,840 B usable), 20 tools cut, 150–300 s → 3.6–35.6 s, and the three Kconfig symbols behind the PSRAM freeze.

---

## Key points to send by Sept 19

**1. You don't start from zero.** The ai_agent framework, TFLite-Micro, LVGL, the ES8311 audio driver, littlefs and USB CDC-NCM networking are all reusable openVela components. They all run together in one firmware image on a real ESP32-S3, not a simulator. The agent's behaviour is a 26-line Markdown Skill file, not C code.

**2. It's a full system, so you can profile and fix it end to end.** On-device inference dropped from 6.75 s to 1.31 s after profiling showed 84% of the time was in CONV_2D. The agent's request was 19,391 bytes, while the network buffers held about 7,840 usable bytes. Removing 20 unused tools took responses from 150–300 s down to 3.6–35.6 s, with 8 of 8 requests succeeding.

**3. The gaps are specific and fixable.** openVela ships NN kernels for ARM (`cmsis-nn`) and HiFi DSPs (`nnlib-hifi4`), but none for Xtensa LX7. We submitted ESP-NN as a fork/PR. There's also a hidden config dependency: `ARCH_HAVE_EXTRA_HEAPS` never appears in a defconfig, yet without it the first agent request froze the whole chip.

---

## Spoken version (~2 minutes)

> "I'm answering as the developer who built VelaPaw, a multi-pet smart feeder, on an ESP32-S3 with openVela.
>
> The first difference is how much I didn't have to write. The agent framework, TensorFlow Lite Micro, LVGL, the audio codec driver, littlefs and USB networking all came from openVela. They run together in one firmware image on real hardware. The agent's proactive behaviour, a feeding digest, is a 26-line Markdown Skill file, not C code.
>
> The second difference is that it behaves like a full system, so you can measure it and fix it. Pet recognition took 6.75 seconds. Profiling showed 84% of that time was in one operator, and optimised kernels brought it down to 1.31 seconds. The agent's requests were 19 kilobytes, but the network buffers held under 8. After we removed 20 unused tools, responses fell from several minutes to between 4 and 36 seconds, and all eight test requests succeeded.
>
> Third, the gaps are specific. openVela has neural-network kernels for ARM and HiFi DSPs, but nothing for the ESP32-S3's LX7 core, so we submitted ESP-NN as a fork. One config symbol never appears in a defconfig, and without it the first agent request froze the whole chip. Both are easy to fix, and fixing them would make the next developer's path much shorter."

That's about 270 words, which fits 2 minutes at a normal speaking pace.

L622: Development-side Skills: the organiser-provided set installed via the .claude manifest was used, of which the ones that materially contributed here were contest-log-collector (AI-coding log collection), kconfig-tweak (editing .config without menuconfig), openvela-build (build flow), submit-pr (submission flow), and the general-purpose artifact-design. The Skill tool fired 17 times across the collected logs.
L623: A persistent memory store of 40+ entries was also maintained, recording across sessions which approaches had been falsified on hardware (for example "CONFIG_RTC kills the USB console", "writing 0x818000 wedges the SoC", "the claim that repeated wapi hangs the console is retracted"). This measurably reduced the cost of re-treading the same ground on a long-running project.
L625: Total token usage
L626: Summed from 35,074 assistant messages carrying usage records:
L627: Input tokens: 340,649
L628: Output tokens: 44,262,781
L629: Cache-creation tokens: 181,608,127
L630: Cache-read tokens: 6,725,913,276
L631: Total: 6,952,124,833 (≈6.95 billion)

Cache reads are 96.7% of the total, which is the characteristic shape of a long-context hardware-debugging project: every "change config → build → flash → read console" round carries the full board context back through inference.
L635: What AI actually contributed, in order of value:
L637: Reframing an apparent software bug as a measurable physical one. All 60 failed rebuilds on the hardware-SPI problem were looking for a cause in software. The turning point was the decision to mirror the SPI pins onto headers, run a ground-truth test first, and decode with a logic analyser. Designing that approach and working through it was a human-AI collaboration; the conclusion — the peripheral is innocent, the problem is panel bit synchronisation — was obtainable only by measurement.
L638: Discriminating between similar-looking symptoms. For example: "whole-frame hue is decisive — a flip or Bayer-phase error can never lose green, so violet means 0x4514, not the flip bits", which pinned in one step a problem that would otherwise have meant blind-testing dozens of registers.
L639: Establishing and applying falsification criteria. Several early "conclusions" in this project were ultimately overturned and explicitly marked as retracted in the memory store (the "repeated wapi hangs the console" claim turned out to be a test-harness artefact; "stale history suppresses tool calls" came from one confounded A/B; "dead TX implies dead clock" was falsified at the register level). Recording what was disproved matters as much as recording what was proved.
L640: Debugging across the hardware-software boundary. The missing ES8311 RX TDM slot map, the ratio between the IOB pool and the request body, the mutual exclusion between PSRAM stacks and the flash cache — none of these sit in a single layer; all required holding kernel configuration, driver registers, and application behaviour simultaneously.

## As a key point

**AI wrote the code; I checked it on the hardware.** About 18,800 lines (C/C++ firmware, host-side Python, the ai_agent patches and the defconfig) were written in Claude Code sessions. My part was building and wiring the board, taking logic-analyser and multimeter readings, doing every flash, and deciding when an AI conclusion was wrong. We kept a memory file of 40+ entries recording what the hardware had disproved, so later sessions didn't repeat dead ends.

## Spoken version (~35 seconds)

> "On AI-assisted development: almost all of the roughly 18,800 lines were written in sessions with Claude Code. My job was the part AI can't do: wiring the board, taking the measurements, flashing it, and deciding when the AI was wrong. That happened more than once. Some early conclusions turned out to be test artefacts, so we kept a memory file of what the hardware had disproved, and later sessions didn't repeat those mistakes. The best example is the display. We did 60 failed rebuilds looking for a software bug. The breakthrough came from putting a logic analyser on the SPI pins, and that showed the bug was in the panel's bit sync, not the code."

- **"~100% AI-written" on its own:** without the next sentence about who checked the work, it sounds like the AI did everything. Always say both together.

## Fitting it into 2 minutes
The organizers asked for 2–3 points. Adding this one on top of the other three runs to about 2.5 minutes. Since AI-assisted development was one of the topics they suggested, I'd use it as point 3 in place of the "gaps" point (ESP-NN and `ARCH_HAVE_EXTRA_HEAPS`). Keep the gaps point as a follow-up in case the moderator asks what openVela is missing.

**Subject:** Re: Roundtable Q3 – Key Points (VelaPaw, Team CircuitForge)

Dear Organizing Committee,

Thank you for inviting me to the roundtable at the openvela AI Hardware Innovation Summit on September 23. I'm glad to take part. Below are my key points for Q3 (openVela's core differentiators compared with traditional RTOSes). They are based on building VelaPaw, a multi-pet smart feeder, on an ESP32-S3 with openVela.

**Key points**

**1. Developers don't start from zero.**
The ai_agent framework, TensorFlow Lite Micro, LVGL, the ES8311 audio driver, littlefs and USB CDC-NCM networking are all reusable openVela components. They run together in one firmware image on real ESP32-S3 hardware, not a simulator. The agent's proactive behaviour is defined in a 26-line Markdown Skill file, not C code.

**2. It's a complete system, so it can be measured and optimised end to end.**
On-device pet recognition dropped from 6.75 s to 1.31 s after profiling showed 84% of the time was in one operator (CONV_2D). The agent's LLM requests were 19,391 bytes, but only about 7,840 bytes of network buffer were usable. Removing 20 unused tools brought response times from 150–300 s down to 3.6–35.6 s, and all 8 test requests succeeded.

**3. AI wrote the code, and people checked it on the hardware.**
Nearly all of the project's roughly 18,800 lines were written in sessions with Claude Code. My part was building and wiring the hardware, taking the measurements, doing every flash, and deciding when an AI conclusion was wrong. We kept a memory file of what the hardware had disproved, so later sessions didn't repeat dead ends.

**Spoken version (about 2 minutes)**

> "I'm answering as the developer who built VelaPaw, a multi-pet smart feeder, on an ESP32-S3 with openVela.
>
> The first difference is how much I didn't have to write. The agent framework, TensorFlow Lite Micro, LVGL, the audio codec driver, littlefs and USB networking all came from openVela. They run together in one firmware image on real hardware. The agent's proactive behaviour, a feeding digest, is a 26-line Markdown Skill file, not C code.
>
> The second difference is that it behaves like a full system, so you can measure it and fix it. Pet recognition took 6.75 seconds. Profiling showed 84% of that time was in one operator, and optimised kernels brought it down to 1.31 seconds. The agent's requests were 19 kilobytes, but the network buffers held under 8. After we removed 20 unused tools, responses fell from several minutes to between 4 and 36 seconds, and all eight test requests succeeded.
>
> Third, AI-assisted development. Almost all of the roughly 18,800 lines were written in sessions with Claude Code. My job was the part AI can't do: wiring the board, taking the measurements, flashing it, and deciding when the AI was wrong. That happened more than once, so we kept a memory file of what the hardware had disproved. The best example is the display. We did 60 failed rebuilds looking for a software bug. The breakthrough came from putting a logic analyser on the SPI pins, and that showed the problem was in the panel's bit sync, not the code."

If the moderator asks a follow-up about gaps, I can also cover two specific ones we hit. openVela ships NN kernels for ARM and HiFi DSPs but none for the ESP32-S3's LX7 core, so we submitted ESP-NN as a fork/PR. And `ARCH_HAVE_EXTRA_HEAPS` never appears in a defconfig, yet without it the first agent request froze the chip.

I look forward to the discussion on September 23.

Best regards,
Kingsley Mbewe
Team CircuitForge (contest2026_043)

The honest answer is: **across boards yes, across architectures no.** Everything in the report ran on one chip family (ESP32-S3), so we shouldn't claim cross-architecture portability.

## What the report supports

- **Across boards, same chip:** L183 says the Waveshare board has "the same SoC as the official ESP32-S3-EYE, so the openVela port and all inference work carry over unchanged." We changed boards because the product needed a touchscreen and a hardware RTC, which the EYE doesn't have.
- **A new board port:** L407 says the Waveshare board had no board support in openVela. We added a full board implementation on top of `esp32s3-devkit`: 1,903 lines of C plus a 205-line defconfig, with drivers for the display, camera, audio and stepper motor.
- **Early work in an emulator:** L118/L541–542 describe an early TFLite-Micro test run in QEMU, not on the S3, which showed CONV_2D taking 84% of the time. The report labels those QEMU figures "not an S3 measurement". The 5× speedup measured later on the S3 confirmed the finding.
- **Across architectures:** there's no evidence. We never moved to ARM or RISC-V. What the report does show is an architecture gap: kernels exist for ARM and HiFi DSPs but not for LX7 (L298).

## Paragraph to add to the email

Add this after point 3, next to the "gaps" follow-up:

> **On portability across boards and architectures:** our code moved across boards, but not across architectures. We picked the Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C because it uses the same SoC as the official ESP32-S3-EYE, so the openVela port and all inference work carried over unchanged. We then added full board support on top of `esp32s3-devkit` (about 1,900 lines of C plus a defconfig) for the touchscreen, camera, audio codec and stepper motor. We also used QEMU for early TFLite-Micro profiling, and the result held up on the real S3. We didn't move to another CPU architecture, and that's where we saw openVela's gap: optimised NN kernels exist for ARM and HiFi DSPs, but not for Xtensa LX7.

> "Across boards, yes. Same chip, different board, so the openVela port and the inference work carried over unchanged, and we added a new board port on top of the devkit. Yes — skipping a single meal is implemented, and it works per pet, per meal slot.

## How it works

The state lives in [ui_lvgl.c:222](D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\app\velapaw\ui\ui_lvgl.c#L222):

```c
static uint8_t g_meal_skipped[VELAPAW_MAX_PETS][VELAPAW_MAX_MEALS];
```

- **To skip:** on the My Pets page, tap any meal row that hasn't been eaten yet. That toggles it off, and tapping again turns it back on ([ui_lvgl.c:1517-1524](D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\app\velapaw\ui\ui_lvgl.c#L1517-L1524)).
- **The row then reads "18:00 skipped"** / "已跳过" ([ui_i18n.c:112](D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\app\velapaw\ui\ui_i18n.c#L112)), instead of "pending" or "waiting for pet".
- **The feeder honours it** in the dispensing gate at [ui_lvgl.c:3968](D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\app\velapaw\ui\ui_lvgl.c#L3968): a skipped slot is passed over, so even if the pet is recognised at the bowl and the meal is due, no food comes out.
- **Other meals are unaffected.** The comment at line 1623 puts it exactly as the report does: "skip meal 2 but still feed 1 and 3".

So the report's claim at L134 ("at most once per meal per day, with any meal individually skippable") is accurate, and so is the plaque description.

## One bug worth knowing about

Skips do not clear at real midnight. They're only cleared in three places:

1. app startup ([ui_lvgl.c:3580](D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\app\velapaw\ui\ui_lvgl.c#L3580))
2. the demo **Next Day** button ([ui_lvgl.c:3680](D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\app\velapaw\ui\ui_lvgl.c#L3680))
3. pet deletion, which shifts the array down

The "eaten" flag next to it stores a date (`g_meal_fed_day[i][k] == today`), so it resets correctly on a real day change. But `g_meal_skipped` is just a flag with no date attached, so a meal skipped today stays skipped tomorrow — and every day after — until someone presses Next Day or the board reboots. This is the same class of bug as the feeding-history day stamp you fixed earlier: state that only advances when the demo button is pressed.

The fix is the same shape: store a date instead of a flag (`long g_meal_skip_day[...]`, compared against `wall_day()`), so a skip applies to one day only. That's a small change, but it touches the dispensing path, so it needs a hardware test and shouldn't be rushed before the 23rd.

For the exhibition it doesn't matter — skips get cleared when the board boots, and the demo won't span midnight.

Here's what's actually in the repo, since that determines what to flash.

## The firmware in the repo

| File | Size | MD5 |
|---|---|---|
| `nuttx.bin` | 1,561,920 | `CE83189340B3422E0BA2F8EB7C9A8A5C` |
| `app/velapaw/infer/model/velapaw.tflite` | 1,436,344 | `4DD42871DEAF990B1BDC3A2E2A3D89DD` |
| `app/velapaw/infer/model/bcs.tflite` | 626,512 | `952500D06D6855B0142422E4E6CC4437` |

`nuttx.bin` is the **Sept 5, 2026 04:45** build, committed in `935b5a7` ("run openVela ai_agent on the board with a custom Skill"). It contains `velapaw`, `ai_agent` and `heartbeat`, so it is the right build — the one the report and demo video describe.

## Why it probably doesn't work after flashing

**`nuttx.bin` is not the whole image.** It writes 0x0–~0x17ec80. The two AI models live in raw flash far past that, at `0x600000` and `0x760000`, and are loaded into PSRAM at boot ([backend_tflm.cc:43](D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\app\velapaw\infer\backend_tflm.cc#L43), [:54](D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\app\velapaw\infer\backend_tflm.cc#L54)).

Flashing only `nuttx.bin` leaves whatever was at those offsets. If the chip was erased, the models are gone, and **the failure is silent**: `tflm_init` returns -1 and nobody checks it. The UI comes up, but recognition never matches, so no food is dispensed. This exact thing happened on 2026-09-03, when both blobs were found fully erased.

## Full flash sequence

Run these on the VM, from the repo directory. Check the port first — this is `/dev/ttyUSB0` on some setups and `/dev/ttyACM0` on others:

```
ls /dev/ttyUSB* /dev/ttyACM* 2>/dev/null
```

Then, with the correct port:

```
esptool.py --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/ttyUSB0 --baud 921600 write_flash \
  0x0      nuttx.bin \
  0x600000 app/velapaw/infer/model/velapaw.tflite \
  0x760000 app/velapaw/infer/model/bcs.tflite
```

If esptool retries on connect, hold BOOT and tap RESET during the retry.

## Verify the models really landed

```
esptool.py --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/ttyUSB0 read_flash 0x600000 0x15E338 /tmp/rb_velapaw.tflite
esptool.py --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/ttyUSB0 read_flash 0x760000 0x98F50  /tmp/rb_bcs.tflite
md5sum /tmp/rb_velapaw.tflite /tmp/rb_bcs.tflite
```

These must come back as `4dd42871deaf990b1bdc3a2e2a3d89dd` and `952500d06d6855b0142422e4e6cc4437`. If they're all `ff` bytes, the models never got written and that's your fault line.

## After flashing

`/data` (littlefs at `0x180000`) survives a `write-flash 0x0`, so the agent's API key, the Skill file and the feeding records should still be there. A **full chip erase wipes all of it**, and the agent then fails with no key. Avoid `erase_flash` unless you're ready to re-provision.

Then on the console, press Enter three times to get `nsh>`, and:

```
velapaw
```

Found it. **The feature isn't in the firmware on your board.** It's not a tap-handling bug.

## Evidence

I scanned the committed `nuttx.bin` (the Sept 5 04:45 build, the one on the board) for the meal-row strings from [ui_i18n.c:110-112](D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\app\velapaw\ui\ui_i18n.c#L110-L112):

| String | In firmware? |
|---|---|
| `  %02d:%02d   pending` | yes |
| `  %02d:%02d   waiting for pet` | yes |
| `  %02d:%02d   skipped` | **no** |

Its neighbours in the same table are there, so the table exists — the skipped entry specifically is absent. The only `skipped` in the whole binary is an mbedTLS error message, and the only 跳过 is in an ai_agent cron template at `0xFA259`. So there's no `S_SKIPPED` string and no `meal_skip_toggle_cb`. Tapping does nothing because nothing is listening.

## Why

The repo source has had the feature since Aug 12 (`af9791d`), but the firmware was built on Sept 5 from the **VM tree**, not from this repo. The VM's copy of `apps/examples/velapaw/` is missing the skip code. The repo and the VM have drifted, and the binary follows the VM.

## What to do

The VM tree is the authoritative build source, so don't blind-copy over it — some fixes exist only there. Diff first. On the VM:

```
diff -ru ~/openvela/apps/examples/velapaw/ui \
         /path/to/contest2026_043_CircuitForge/app/velapaw/ui
```

If the only differences are the skip feature, copy those two files across:

```

Then clear the stale-build state and rebuild:

```

cd ~/openvela && ./build.sh esp32s3-devkit:waveshare_lcd -j4

Then flash just the firmware (the models at `0x600000` / `0x760000` stay put):

```

```

Check the port name first, and hold BOOT + tap RESET if esptool retries.

## Two things to know

1. **The repo's `nuttx.bin` is also missing this feature**, so it needs recommitting after the rebuild. Worth doing before the 23rd so the repo matches what you demo.
2. **The midnight bug from earlier still applies.** Once it's running, a skipped meal stays skipped past midnight, since `g_meal_skipped` holds a flag with no date. It only clears on reboot or the Next Day button. That won't show up in the exhibition demo.

# skipmeal — per-slot "skip this meal" toggle on My Pets · ⭐ CURRENTLY ON THE BOARD

`nuttx-skipmeal.bin` · 1,062,112 bytes
`5210e00bdb99ba473ca9acb6ffaf0d6ebbb0ab3a3bc0ad60debe03f32015fbcf`

Source (changed files only): `src/ui_lvgl.c`, `src/ui_i18n.c`, `src/ui_i18n.h`.
Hashes in `SHA256SUMS.txt`. Built on top of `../2026-08-08-b82r-rebuild/`
(same `.config` — audio debug ON — untouched this session).

## What it is

Adds a per-(pet, meal-slot) "skip today" toggle to the My Pets card, so the
owner can say "don't feed meal 2 today, but still feed 1 and 3" without
touching the schedule itself.

- Tapping any not-yet-eaten meal row (waiting-for-pet or pending) toggles it
  skipped; tapping again un-skips it. Rows already marked "ate" are not
  tappable — you can't skip food already dispensed.
- A skipped row shows "skipped" instead of "waiting"/"pending".
- The recognition-gated dispense gate (Model B) treats a skipped slot the
  same as an already-eaten one: it will never dispense for that slot today.
- Skips are **not sticky** — they reset automatically at the same point
  `g_meal_fed_day` resets: app boot and the "Next Day" button. There's no
  wall-clock midnight timer in this app (day rollover is the manual Next Day
  button), so that's what "resets at night" maps to here.

## Source changes (all in `app/velapaw/ui/`)

- `ui_i18n.h` / `ui_i18n.c`: new string `S_SKIPPED` ("  %02d:%02d   skipped" /
  "  %02d:%02d   已跳过"), same shape as the existing `S_WAITING`/`S_PENDING`.
- `ui_lvgl.c`:
  - new `static uint8_t g_meal_skipped[VELAPAW_MAX_PETS][VELAPAW_MAX_MEALS];`
    next to the existing `g_meal_fed_*` arrays.
  - new `meal_skip_toggle_cb()`, placed just above `refresh_pets()`, flips the
    flag (pet/slot packed into the LVGL event's `user_data` as
    `pet * VELAPAW_MAX_MEALS + slot`) and calls `refresh_pets()`.
  - `refresh_pets()`'s meal-timeline loop: not-yet-eaten rows are now
    `LV_OBJ_FLAG_CLICKABLE` with `lv_obj_set_ext_click_area(ml, 10)` for a
    usable touch target, and render "skipped" when the flag is set.
  - the Model-B dispense gate gained `if (g_meal_skipped[m.id][k]) continue;`

Yes — I checked it from Windows, and the answer is good news.

## What I found

There's a snapshot at `velapaw-snapshots/2026-08-08-skipmeal/` containing the exact three source files from when this feature was built and working on the board on Aug 8. Its `RESTORE.md` even says "⭐ CURRENTLY ON THE BOARD" at the time.

- `ui_i18n.c` and `ui_i18n.h` — **byte-identical** to the repo

Then I checked all 70 English UI strings from the repo source against the firmware on your board. **Exactly one is missing: `"  %02d:%02d   skipped"`.** Every other UI string is present.

So the VM's UI source and the repo's differ in essentially one thing: the skip feature. The feature was lost during the Aug 10 b82-camerafix rebuild, which reconstructed the tree from older snapshots, and it was never put back. That's why the Sept 5 build doesn't have it.

That also means copying the repo's UI files over the VM's is safe — there's no VM-only UI work to lose.

**Symptom (2026-09-22):** on the board, tapping a not-yet-eaten meal row on My Pets did
nothing — no "skipped" label. Everything else in the app worked.

**Root cause: the feature was never in the flashed firmware, it was not broken.**
It shipped and ran on 2026-08-08 (`D:\openVela\velapaw-snapshots\2026-08-08-skipmeal\`,
whose RESTORE.md still claimed "⭐ CURRENTLY ON THE BOARD"), was lost in the

`[Text.Encoding]::GetEncoding(28591)` (byte-preserving; `Latin1` does not exist in
.NET Framework 4.x) and check *all ~70* English i18n strings. Exactly one was missing —
`"  %02d:%02d   skipped"`. One missing string out of a whole table pinpoints the one
source change absent from the build. Checking a single string proves nothing.

`ui_lvgl.c` is *ahead* of `dev-ai-contest-2026`: it heap-allocates `g_img565`,
`g_thumb565` and `g_voice_audio` (`malloc`, was `.bss`), which is the DRAM the
ai_agent integration needed. A file copy silently reverts that. Diff before copying,
always, and patch surgically instead. `ui_i18n.c`/`ui_i18n.h` *are* safe to copy —
their only diff from the VM copy is the `S_SKIPPED` row.

validated on Windows (reverse-apply → forward-apply → `diff -q` identical), pasted to
the VM as a heredoc, `patch -l -p0` (the `-l` matters: two hunks contain blank context

the mbedTLS string, the build didn't take); `grep -ac "%02d:%02d   skipped"` must be 1.

`python -m esptool` (5.3.1). Transfer the image with the user's own `python3 -m
http.server 8000` on the VM (VMnet8: VM = 192.168.160.128, host = .1) and

`0x600000`/`0x760000` and `/data` at `0x180000` survive.

dateless `uint8_t`, so a skip does *not* expire at real midnight — only on reboot or
the demo Next Day button. Fix would be `long g_meal_skip_day[][]` compared against
`wall_day()`, mirroring `g_meal_fed_day`. Related: [[velapaw-feeding-history-daystamp]].

58	**The node names are the proof of success.** With the `#elif` taken,
59	`board_i2sdev_initialize()` is compiled out — nothing else can register those nodes, so
60	`pcm0`/`pcm_in0` existing *is* confirmation the codec init returned OK.

62	## The link failure that cost the most time
63	
64	`undefined reference to nxmutex_lock/nxmutex_unlock` from `esp32s3_i2s.o`, preceded by an
65	`implicit declaration` warning. **Cause: the VM's `esp32s3_i2s.c` was missing
66	`#include <nuttx/mutex.h>`.** `CONFIG_LIBC_SEM_MUTEX_NOINLINE` is **off**, so those are
67	`static inline` bodies in the header — no exported symbol exists anywhere; an implicit
68	declaration turns them into extern calls that can never resolve. Adding the include is
69	the entire fix.
70	
71	**Why:** I first "verified" the include was present by grepping `D:\openVela\nuttx` — the
72	*Windows* tree, which is not what the VM builds. The two `nuttx` checkouts are at
73	different revisions (Windows also carries a duplicate `#include <nuttx/semaphore.h>`).
74	**How to apply:** for anything about a build, grep the VM tree, never the Windows one.
75	Line numbers are the tell — the error said 2790, Windows said 2792.
76	
77	## VM-only patches — a `repo sync` silently loses all three
78	
79	None is inside `contest2026_043_CircuitForge/`, so nothing tracks them. **`~/fix_vm_patches.sh`
80	applies all three, idempotently — run it before every build that changed config.**
81	1. `nuttx/arch/xtensa/src/esp32s3/esp32s3_i2s.c` → add `#include <nuttx/mutex.h>`.
82	2. `nuttx/drivers/audio/es8311.c` → the same missing include (anchor on
83	   `<nuttx/audio/es8311.h>`). **Upstream bug in this revision, not tree drift** — the
84	   Windows copy lacks it too.
85	3. esp-hal `LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED` → `SP_UNLOCKED` (see [[velapaw-i18n]]; reverted by
86	   the re-clone that *any* Kconfig change triggers). Only rewrite the `= 0` form; leave
87	   `portMUX_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED` alone.
88	4. `nuttx/drivers/audio/es8311.c` → **`es8311_configure()` reports success as `-ERANGE`**
89	   (`loopback` → `Error loopback test: 34`). `ret` is pre-loaded `-ERANGE` and cleared
90	   only by `ret = es8311_setsamplerate(priv) == -ENOTTY ? OK : ret;` — a successful call
91	   returns 0, `0 == -ENOTTY` is false, so the error survives. Four sites (setsamplerate +
92	   setbitspersample × INPUT/OUTPUT). Rewrite to
93	   `ret = es8311_setX(priv); if (ret == -ENOTTY) ret = OK;`. Leave the two bare calls in
94	   `es8311_reset()` alone. Upstream bug.
95	
96	🔴 **Ordering: config-changing build = build → fix → build, NOT fix → build.** The
97	esp-hal re-clone happens *during* the build, so patching first is wiped and the unpatched
98	file compiles. A first failure on `clk_ctrl_os.c:39 … invalid initializer` is expected.
99	The script's output looks correct either way — it reports the tree *before* the re-clone.

101	**Why `fix_vm_patches.sh` replaced `~/fix_hal.sh`:** the old one did `grep -rl … | head -1`
102	and so patched `modem_clock.c` while the real failure was `clk_ctrl_os.c:27`. **How to
103	apply:** loop over *every* match (`while read -r f`), never `head -1`.
104	
105	Verified over the console: **`/dev/audio/` contains `pcm0` (TX) and `pcm_in0` (RX)** —
106	both directions registered. `pcm_in0` is what the wake-word path will read.

133	## Step 3 IN PROGRESS — PA_CTRL done, ear test not yet passing
134	
135	`PA_CTRL` ✅: it's **TCA9554 EXIO7, not a GPIO** ([[velapaw-hardware]]), so the ES8311
136	driver can't reach it. `board_speaker_enable(bool)` added to `esp32s3_st7789.c` beside the
137	existing `g_ioe` handle, asserted at boot under `#ifdef CONFIG_AUDIO_ES8311`; confirmed by
138	`[velapaw] speaker amp enabled (PA_CTRL = EXIO7)`. Exported, not inlined — the app will
139	gate it per-playback later (a permanently-on amp idles and hisses).
140	
141	🔴 **`nxlooper` can't allocate buffers without `CONFIG_AUDIO_DRIVER_SPECIFIC_BUFFERS=y`.**
142	`loopback` returns clean, nothing is audible, and `dmesg` shows
143	`nxlooper_loopthread: ERROR: Could not allocate buffer 0` → the loop thread exits at once,
144	so **nothing ever reaches the codec** and neither the amp nor the mic is implicated.
145	Chain: es8311 answers `AUDIOIOC_GETBUFFERINFO` with `Unhandled ioctl: 4106` → `audio.c:1267`
146	sets `upper->nbuffers` *only* on a successful lower-half answer, so it stays 0 →
147	`audio_allocbuffer()` (`audio.c:786`) opens `if (upper->periods >= upper->nbuffers) return 0;`
148	→ `0>=0` → nxlooper wants `sizeof(buf_desc)`, gets 0. **Not memory pressure** — the
149	allocator refuses before trying. es8311 already implements the handler (`es8311.c:1806`);
150	the `case` is just `#ifdef`'d out. Upstream Kconfig miss: `AUDIO_ES8388` has
151	`select AUDIO_DRIVER_SPECIFIC_BUFFERS`, `AUDIO_ES8311` doesn't, though
152	`ES8311_BUFFER_SIZE`/`ES8311_NUM_BUFFERS` exist unconditionally. **One defconfig line, no
153	source patch.** 4 × 8 KB/direction; ≈256 ms per buffer at 16 kHz mono, so ~1 s echo delay
154	is expected on the ear test.
155	
156	**Back out before shipping:** `CONFIG_DEBUG_AUDIO{,_ERROR,_INFO,_WARN}`,
157	`CONFIG_DEBUG_FEATURES`, `CONFIG_RAMLOG_BUFSIZE=16384`.
158	
159	## RAMLOG / NSH gotchas that cost real time
160	**`dmesg` doesn't drain the buffer, and a full buffer drops new messages.** At the 1024 B
161	default, `DEBUG_AUDIO_INFO` filled it during boot, so nothing post-boot was ever recorded
162	and three `dmesg` runs returned byte-identical text — which reads as "nothing is
163	happening" when the truth is "nothing is being logged". `CONFIG_RAMLOG_BUFSIZE=16384`
164	fixes it; RAMLOG is `.bss`, so `nuttx.bin` is unchanged.
165	
166	NSH has **no pipe** and its `dmesg` takes **no arguments** (`dmesg | grep …` → "too many
167	arguments"); `dmesg` is not an `nxlooper` command — type it at `nsh>` only. End a loopback
168	with `q`, not `stop`: `quit` stops the loop itself, one blocking call instead of two.
169	
170	## 🔴 THE RX STALL — ROOT CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-03 (patch #25)
171	
172	`loopback` ran but **RX delivered 0 bytes forever** — `nbytes=0` on every dequeue, across
173	~15 builds. **Cause: nothing in `esp32s3_i2s.c` ever writes `I2S_RX_TDM_CTRL_REG`.**
174	`i2s_txchannels()` programs `I2S_TX_TDM_TOT_CHAN_NUM` + per-slot `CHANn_EN` for TX, but
175	`i2s_rxchannels()` is a **pure no-op** — it stores `priv->channels` and programs *no*
176	registers. So RX sits at the reset default `TOT_CHAN_NUM=0` = **one slot per frame**,
177	while `RX_CONF1` describes a **two-slot 32-bit frame**. The receiver clocks and completes
178	frames but every slot is discarded.
179	
180	**Fix (keep — real upstream defect):** in `i2s_configure()`, mirror `i2s_txchannels`:
181	set `RX_TDM_TOT_CHAN_NUM=1`, clear low 16 bits, set
182	`I2S_RX_TDM_PDM_CHAN0_EN|CHAN1_EN`, pulse `I2S_RX_UPDATE`. → `nbytes=4092` immediately.
183	
184	⚠️ **The signature that misleads:** every I²S register reads *perfectly healthy*.
185	`RX_START=1`, clocks/dividers/framing/bit-width all correct, GDMA bound (`perisel=3`),
186	descriptors loaded, FSM running. `I2S_RX_DONE_INT_RAW` even **sets** — RX really is
187	completing frames. The only tells are `DMA_IN_INT_RAW` bit7 `INFIFO_UDF_L1` +
188	`EMPTY_L1` (GDMA starving) and `IN_DONE` never firing.
189	
190	**How to apply:** when RX completes frames but delivers no bytes, check the **TDM slot
191	map** before anything else. Don't chase clocks, WS width, descriptors or the codec —
192	all were ruled out at the cost of a dozen builds. **Immunity to change is itself
193	evidence**: bit-identical dumps across four unrelated fixes meant the data was being
194	discarded downstream of everything we were touching.
195	
196	**Two throwaway diagnostics that cracked it** (both reverted; keep the technique):
197	- **Pad-share loopback**: set `DINPIN=DOUTPIN=16` + `configgpio(din, INPUT_FUNCTION_2|OUTPUT)`
198	  when they match. Feeds TX's own data into RX with the codec out of circuit — proves the
199	  digital path without a scope. Safe *only* on DOUT (16, codec input, high-Z); never on
200	  DIN (14) — driving the codec's output pin is contention.
201	- **Force RX master** (clear `I2S_RX_SLAVE_MOD`) to test whether `I2S_SIG_LOOPBACK` is
202	  really sharing TX's BCLK/WS. It was; RX was fine as a slave.
203	
204	Add to `~/fix_vm_patches.sh` as patch 5 — it's in `nuttx/`, so `repo sync` eats it.
205	
206	**Doc drift found en route:** `hardware/README.md:32-41` and `docs/ENGINEERING.md:86` /
207	`ENGINEERING_zh.md:58` still show the stepper on **GPIO12/13/15** with the justification
208	*"VelaPaw uses no audio, so they're free"*. **Stale — it moved to GPIO9/10/11/43**
209	(`board/esp32s3_st7789.c:422-425`), and those docs need correcting. 12/13/15 are I²S
210	MCLK/BCLK/WS. See [[velapaw-stepper-bringup]].
211	
212	## 🔴 RX_HUNG: only a REAL power cycle clears it (2026-08-03)
213	
214	Capture died mid-session and stayed dead across three flashes — including a
215	reflash of the **exact binary that had worked an hour earlier** (md5-verified).
216	Symptom set, bit-identical every run:
217	`i2sraw=0000000f` (**bit2 = RX_HUNG**), `eofdes=00000000` (RX DMA never reached
218	a single successful EOF), `raw=000000a0`, `fifo=0f810f16`, `act=1 pend=1 done=0`,
219	and **zero `VP: mic` lines**. TX was healthy throughout.
220	
221	**Fix: unplug USB, wait ~10 s, replug.** `esptool`'s RTS reset — and the board's
222	RESET button — never drop power to the ES8311 or the AXP, so the codec stays
223	latched. After a true cold start the same binary ran clean immediately.
224	
225	**Why this cost two wasted build cycles:** the failure began right after a meter
226	patch, so I blamed my own change and shipped two "fixes" for it. The register
227	evidence was in the *first* failing log and I misread the RXDUMP as scheduling
228	jitter instead of decoding it. **How to apply:** (1) when RX stalls, decode
229	`i2sraw` bit2 and `eofdes` *before* forming any theory — they say outright
230	whether the peripheral ever received anything; (2) `eofdes=0` means the failure
231	is upstream of every buffer, so nothing that runs *after* a buffer completes
232	(the meter, the callback) can possibly be the cause; (3) reflashing the
233	last-known-good binary is a near-free control test — run it FIRST, not third.
234	
235	Config registers (`rxconf`, `eofnum`, `rxclkm`, `rxdiv`, `rxconf1`, `rxtdm`,
236	`txtdm`) and both descriptors were **identical** between working and hung runs.
237	When only *status* differs and config doesn't, stop reading the source.

10	
11	`apps/examples/velapaw/voice/mic.c` — 1 s of 16 kHz mono for `micro_speech`.
12	
13	**WORKING on hardware, build 52 (2026-08-05):** live "yes" **0.996**, "no"
14	**0.750**, silence correctly rejected. Every earlier result was weak
15	(b46: yes 0.539, no 0.715) because of the two defects below, both in capture,
16	neither in the model.
17	
18	## 🔴 RX delivers TWO slots and one of them is dead
19	
20	`I2S_RX_MONO` marks the second slot invalid but does **not** remove it from
21	the stream — both slots reach the FIFO and the DMA, with the invalid one
22	zero-filled. Buffers read `[sample, 0, sample, 0, ...]`. This is not 32-bit
23	slot padding: `i2s_set_datawidth()` programs 16-bit slots
24	(`CHAN_BITS = HALF_SAMPLE_BITS = data_width`). It is VelaPaw patch #25:
25	`TOT_CHAN_NUM=1` (two slots) + `CHAN0_EN|CHAN1_EN` + `I2S_RX_MONO`.
26	
27	Consequence: a 16000-`int16` window was **0.5 s of audio with a zero between
28	every sample** — a mirrored spectrum landing inside micro_speech's mel bins.
29	Fix is `MIC_STRIDE 2` — keep one `int16` in two, in `mic_collect()`.
30	
31	### ⚠️ The live slot flips PER CAPTURE, not per build
32	
33	Build 52, one boot: capture 1 slot 0, capture 2 slot 0, capture 3 **slot 1**.
34	Every capture re-arms RX and the first sample lands wherever the frame is.
35	Hardcoding slot 0 makes a capture come back all zeros and look like a dead
36	mic. `mic_data_phase()` measures it, per capture, by counting **exact zeros**
37	— the dead slot is 0 to the bit while the live slot has an ADC noise floor
38	even in a silent room. It returns −1 for an all-zero buffer (RX emits a few
39	while warming up) so the phase is settled off the first buffer with content,
40	not a coin flip.
41	
42	## 🔴 Audio buffers live in PSRAM and the driver does no cache maintenance
43	
44	`apb->samp` addresses are `0x3C5x_xxxx` = the external-memory window
45	(`CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPIRAM=y`, `CONFIG_MM_REGIONS=2`). `esp32s3_i2s.c` has **no**
46	invalidate/writeback/barrier anywhere. So **reusing a buffer inside one
47	window returns a stale cached copy**: first delivery misses cache and reads
48	what DMA wrote, the copy pulls 4 KB into DCache, and ~500 ms later the same
49	buffer hits those warm lines. Signature: an 8-segment profile that repeats
50	with a period equal to the pool depth, and identical samples at the same
51	`apb` pointer.
52	
53	**Fix = never reuse a buffer inside a window.** `GETBUFFERINFO`'s `nbuffers`
54	is a *suggestion*, not a cap — `ALLOCBUFFER` is per-call. `MIC_WANT_BUFS 18`
55	(one delivery = 4092 B = 2046 `int16` = 1023 usable samples after stride, so
56	16000 needs 16 + `MIC_SKIP_BUFS`).
57	
58	### The follow-on trap: a deep pool overruns the quiesce budget
59	
60	Requeueing every accepted buffer left ~17 in flight; one buffer is 128 ms, so
61	draining needs 2.3 s against a 1 s budget sized when the pool was 4. Quiesce
62	timed out, the *next* capture armed with 6 free buffers, and they recycled 3×
63	— reintroducing the cache bug. Two fixes together:
64	- requeue only when `skipped + seq >= nrecbufs - 1` (self-adjusting: a capped
65	  pool still finishes by falling back to recycling)
66	- `MIC_QUIESCE_TRIES 80` (4 s) — a ceiling, not a cost
67	
68	## The repeat-capture bug was PROCESS EXIT, not I2S
69	
70	Each `velapaw kws mic` is a **separate builtin task**. Flat build, so statics
71	(`g_mic`) survive, but **fds do not** — NuttX closes them at task exit, so run
72	2 found `open == true` and got **`-9` (EBADF)**. Guard the session with the
73	owning pid; if `g_mic.owner != getpid()`, `memset` and reopen — **never
74	`close()` those fds**, the numbers belong to someone else now. Test repeat
75	capture *in one process* (`velapaw kws mic [reps]`); the product captures from
76	the long-lived UI task, which does not exit.
77	
78	Signatures: `es8311_getcoeff`/`setsamplerate` spam **at the nsh prompt between
79	runs** = the kernel closing the devices. `ps` showing no `es8311` threads after
80	a "failed" run = the task is gone, nothing leaked.
81	
82	## ⏳ STILL OPEN: `-110` on session reopen
83	
84	A second `velapaw kws mic` in the same boot times out with `0/32000 bytes`.
85	Reliable, not intermittent — reproduced on builds 48–52. **Only a cold power
86	cycle clears it** (RTS reset does not). Not product-blocking: the feeder holds
87	one session in the long-lived UI task. **Test one `velapaw kws mic 3` per
88	boot.**
89	
90	### 🔴 It bites the PRODUCT path too — never run the CLI before the dialog
91	
92	Build 67/68 (2026-08-06): running `velapaw kws mic 1` and *then* opening the
93	voice dialog puts the UI worker's session into exactly this state —
94	`rec 0/18  play 1/1  phase -1  got 0/32000`. The CLI task's session teardown
95	is the trigger; the worker is just the next opener. **This invalidated two
96	builds' worth of hardware tests** while it was read as a new bug.
97	
98	Test rule: **cold power cycle, then go straight to the feature.** The CLI is
99	not a free warm-up. Head 18 / tail 0 = every buffer reached es8311's pendq and
100	none came back — that pair is the signature, distinct from a real timeout.
101	
102	## 🔴 OPEN: the first capture of a boot intermittently stalls
103	
104	Signature (b70, and identically b66):
105	
106	    caps 1  lastret -999   lasterr -110   mic stage 32 (session-close)
107	    mic open0 pid 4 seq 1 ... bufs 18  ret 0     <- one session, opened fine
108	    mic fail got 0/32000  phase -1
109	    mic fail rec 1/19  play 1/1 (tail/head)
110	
111	RX accepted 19 enqueues and returned **one** buffer, which was silent. TX was
112	enqueued once, returned once, never requeued.
113	
114	⚠️ **It is INTERMITTENT, not reset-gated.** A tap of RESET reliably reproduces
115	it, but a cold power cycle does **not** reliably clear it — cold boots fail too
116	(user-confirmed 2026-08-07, correcting an earlier "cold works / RESET fails"
117	reading). So a single passing boot proves nothing; only counters do.
118	
119	### 🔴 The "dead TX ⇒ dead clock" story is FALSIFIED — don't rebuild it
120	
121	It fits the counters and it is wrong. Read in `esp32s3_i2s.c` (clean b68):
122	
123	- Full duplex does set `I2S_SIG_LOOPBACK`, and **RX genuinely is a slave on
124	  TX's BCLK/WS** — that half is confirmed.
125	- But **patch #16 already clears `I2S_TX_STOP_EN`**, the bit that gates BCLK/WS
126	  off when the TX FIFO empties. Its own comment says exactly that.
127	- And **`I2S_TX_START` is never cleared when the TX queue drains.** Set at
128	  `:724`, cleared only in `i2s_tx_channel_stop()` at `:2521`;
129	  `i2s_txdma_start()` returns `OK` on an empty pend queue without touching it.
130	
131	So after the primed silence buffer completes, the clock keeps running.
132	**Requeueing TX (b71's patch) cannot be the fix** — that was caught before
133	spending a build on it. Two neighbouring theories died in the same read:
134	`i2s_configure()` asserts/releases `SYSTEM_I2S0_RST` at `:1559`, so **no I2S
135	register state survives a warm reset**; and the failing boot still reports
136	`reccfg 1 recstart 5 playstart 5 bufs 18 ret 0`, so **codec init is not
137	failing** (the `es8311 -22` spam is cosmetic — see below).
138	
139	### What is actually left
140	
141	`i2s_rx_interrupt()` does `if (bfdesc == inlink) { sq_remfirst(&priv->rx.act); … }`
142	**with no else branch**. One mismatched EOF descriptor strands the container in
143	`rx.act` forever, and from then on every `i2s_rxdma_start()` bails at
144	`if (!sq_empty(&priv->rx.act)) return OK;`. That is exactly `rec 1/19`.
145	
146	### 🔴 …and that is FALSIFIED TOO — patch #31 is dead, by measurement
147	
148	Patch **#33** (build b76, measurement only: non-static counters
149	`g_velapaw_rx_eof/match/miss/empty/start/busy` + `velapaw_i2s_rxdbg()` reading
150	`RX_CONF`/`TX_CONF`/`RXEOF_NUM`, surfaced in the `velapaw voice` probe;
151	`nuttx-b76-measure.bin` sha256 `7cf95e79…`, 1,061,144 B). A stalled boot reads:
152	
153	    i2s eof 1 match 1 miss 0 empty 0  start 2 busy 2
154	    i2s rxconf 0008962c txconf 08089204 rxeofn 4092
155	
156	**`miss 0` — the descriptor walk NEVER desyncs.** Do not reapply #31 for this
157	fault; its `else` branch is still a defensible latent-bug fix, but it is not
158	this bug.
159	
160	**`start 2 busy 2` means only THREE buffers ever reached the I2S driver**, out
161	of the 19 the app enqueued. Timeline: buf1 → `start` (act empty, armed);
162	buf2, buf3 → `busy` (act non-empty, parked in `rx.pend`); one EOF for buf1 →
163	`match`, act empties → buf2 armed (`start`=2); **then nothing, ever.**
164	
165	So the `rec 1/19` pile-up in **es8311's pendq is a SYMPTOM, not the cause** —
166	es8311 stops forwarding because I2S stops completing. The real fault is one
167	line deeper: **RX is armed for buf2 and its DMA never signals EOF.**
168	
169	Registers say the engine is not misconfigured: `RX_START` set, `TX_START` set,
170	`TX_STOP_EN` clear (patch #16 holding), loopback set, `rxeofn 4092` correct.
171	Bit positions since **verified** against the VM's `hardware/esp32s3_i2s.h` and
172	`esp32s3_dma.h`: `I2S_RX_START` BIT(2), `I2S_RX_SLAVE_MOD` BIT(3),
173	`I2S_RX_MONO` BIT(5), `I2S_TX_STOP_EN` BIT(13), `I2S_SIG_LOOPBACK` BIT(27);
174	GDMA `IN_INT_RAW` BIT(0) `IN_DONE`, BIT(1) `IN_SUC_EOF`, BIT(4) `IN_DSCR_EMPTY`,
175	BIT(5) `INFIFO_FULL_WM`, BIT(7) `INFIFO_UDF_L1`. So `intraw 000000a0` is
176	**bits 5 + 7**, and `DSCR_EMPTY` (bit 4) is clear in every dump — a third-party
177	analysis that read bit 7 as `DSCR_EMPTY` was wrong on the naming.
178

189	### ✅ SOLVED (b80): the failure path used to be terminal — it isn't now

194	  cleared only after close returns, so every later caller got `-EBUSY` and
195	  exactly one capture was ever attempted per boot. **Fix (b80): don't close on
196	  failure.** The `failed:` path now kicks the RX channel, flushes the mq, holds
197	  the session open, clears `g_mic_busy` and returns the error.

199	  capture. **Fix (b79):** count failures, sleep 200 ms, `continue`; disable
200	  voice only after `VOICE_MAX_CAPFAIL 3` *consecutive* failures.

367	## b84–b87: WHO arms the mic, and WHEN the first capture happens
368	
369	**b84 removed the Recognize tab's voice arming** — it was a second, spoken
370	feeding path (`voice_apply()` → `velapaw_feeder_dispense()`) that contradicted

373	device**, and `voice_apply`, `voice_idle_text`, `g_voice_lbl`,

376	That removal exposed two things Recognize had been providing **by accident**:
377	
378	1. **Readiness.** `vsched_tick()` will not prompt until `g_voice_ready`, set in
379	   exactly one place — after a capture **succeeds**. Standing on Recognize had

386	   **b86 gives the warm-up its own counter** (`g_voice_warmfail`) that never

437	## ✅ SOLVED: the `es8311 -22` boot spam is cosmetic — never chase it
438	
439	    es8311_getcoeff: MCLK = 4096000 and samplerate = 48000 not supported
440	    es8311_setsamplerate: Failed to set sample rate: -22
441	
442	The driver does it to itself. `es8311.c:2153` sets
443	`priv->samprate = ES8311_DEFAULT_SAMPRATE` (48000), then `:2191` calls
444	`es8311_setsamplerate()` during init while MCLK is 4096000 (= 256 × 16000).
445	`getcoeff(4096000, 48000)` has no table entry → `-22`. The real rate is
446	programmed later from `caps->ac_controls.hw[0]`, and `:1039` already calls
447	`es8311_reset()` *before* `:1046`'s `setsamplerate()`. **It appears in working
448	boots too**, so its presence in a failing log means nothing. This misled a
449	third-party analysis into proposing an ES8311 power-up clock race; that was
450	rejected on evidence.
451	
452	## Session shape
453	
454	Open, configure, `AUDIOIOC_START` **once**; each capture only enqueues and
455	collects. Between captures the session is running but idle. Free-running RX is
456	not an option: `mq_maxmsg = nbuffers + 8`, so with no reader the driver's
457	`mq_send` would drop buffer pointers. `mic_flush_mq()` before each re-arm.
458	
459	⚠️ **`apb->nbytes` is read by the driver *during* the enqueue ioctl** — the
460	caller sets it: record side `0`, playback side `nmaxbytes`. Zeroing it in a
461	shared helper silently sends a zero-length TX buffer → no clock → hang. TX
462	must stay primed; RX borrows BCLK/WS from TX (see [[velapaw-audio-bringup]]).
463	
464	⚠️ Do not conflate this with the falsified theory above. A **zero-length first**
465	TX buffer means `I2S_TX_START` is never set, so the clock never starts — real.
466	TX **draining after** a good buffer is harmless, because `TX_START` stays set
467	and `#16` cleared `TX_STOP_EN`.

11	Audio *quality* tuning on the VelaPaw board, after [[velapaw-audio-bringup]] solved the RX stall (patch #25, the RX TDM slot map).
12	
13	## Never judge this by ear on `nxlooper loopback`
14	
15	The mic and speaker are inches apart on the same board, so loopback is an
16	acoustic feedback loop. Loop gain crossing unity sounds exactly like "noise,
17	can't hear my voice" and it moves with any gain change, which makes ear
18	testing actively misleading. **Measure the samples instead.** The `VP: mic`
19	probe in `esp32s3_i2s.c`'s RX worker (inserted just before
20	`/* Perform the RX transfer done callback */`, thread context so `syslog` is
21	safe) reports per buffer: `peak`, `mean` |sample|, signed `dc`, `rail` (count
22	>= 32000) and `m8` (count == -32768).
23	
24	Note `peak=32768` is not a real magnitude — it means a sample is exactly
25	`-32768` (0x8000), because negating it overflows back to itself.
26	
27	## The ES8311 gain chain (this is what was wrong)
28	
29	- `ES8311_SYSTEM_REG14` bits[3:0] = **analog PGA**, 3 dB/step.
30	  `es8311_start` wrote `0x1a` = 0xA = **30 dB, the maximum**.
31	- `ES8311_ADC_REG16` bits[2:0] = **digital scale-up**, 6 dB/step.
32	  `es8311_reset` wrote `0x24` = 4 = **24 dB**.
33	- Stock total was **54 dB**, which railed the ADC on every buffer *under
34	  loopback*. Retuned to `REG14=0x18` (24 dB) + `REG16=0x20` (0 dB) =
35	  **24 dB total**. ⚠️ **See the correction below — that retune was measured
36	  on loopback and was an overcorrection.**
37	- `ES8311_ADC_REG17` (ADC digital volume) is **clobbered to `0xbf` (0 dB) by
38	  `es8311_start` on every start**, so `CONFIG_ES8311_INPUT_INITVOLUME` does
39	  nothing. Don't try to tune input level with it.
40	- `ES8311_DAC_REG32` (output) comes from `CONFIG_ES8311_OUTPUT_INITVOLUME`
41	  via `29*ln(v)`. Unity is `0xBF`; 400 -> `0xAD` = **-9 dB**, 1000 -> `0xC8`
42	  = **+4.5 dB**. Default 400 is quiet.
43	
44	## Measured, at 24 dB gain (good)
45	
46	- Silence: `peak` 2-10, `mean` 0, `rail` 0 — an essentially perfect floor.
47	- Speech: `mean` ~2000-2600 (about **-22 dBFS**), `rail` up to ~32/2046
48	  (~1.5% peak clipping, mild). Clean enough for micro_speech.
49	- `dc` swings +-1500 over ~1 s periods = sub-10 Hz acoustic coupling, not a
50	  true DC offset. Eats headroom; the ES8311 high-pass could remove it.
51	- Under sustained loopback it gets much worse: `mean=9527 dc=-9511`, i.e.
52	  essentially every sample on one side of zero, which is what drives the
53	  occasional `rail=1..2`. **Loopback-only** — nothing plays back the mic in
54	  the real path, and `micro_speech`'s lowest mel bin is ~125 Hz, so the model
55	  would never see it even if it were there. Not worth fixing for the contest.
56	
57	## 🔴 CORRECTION (2026-08-05): 24 dB was an overcorrection — use 30 dB
58	
59	Everything in the "Measured, at 24 dB gain" section above was taken with
60	loopback running, which this same file warns is acoustically misleading. It
61	was. Measured on the **real** path (`velapaw kws mic`, nothing playing back):
62	
63	- Speech peaked at ~**300 counts** against a noise floor of 2 — about **1% of
64	  full scale**, i.e. far too quiet for `micro_speech`, not "clean".
65	- The railed samples that drove the retune were **not acoustic clipping**.
66	  They are a **start-of-stream transient at a FIXED sample index** (build 42:
67	  both probes peaked at index 57; build 44: `peak=32768@127`; build 45:
68	  `peak=32768@43`). Acoustic content does not land on a fixed index — that
69	  signature is the tell. See [[velapaw-mic-capture]] for the warm-up fix.
70	- Restoring the digital stage to **30 dB (total 54 dB again)** gives speech
71	  at **3830–5399 counts with `rail 0`** and correct keyword recognition.
72	
73	**Do it from the app, not the driver.** `AUDIOIOC_CONFIGURE` with
74	`ac_type = AUDIO_TYPE_FEATURE`, `ac_format.hw = AUDIO_FU_INP_GAIN`,
75	`ac_controls.hw[0] = 30` reaches `es8311_setmicgain` → `ES8311_ADC_REG16`.
76	No driver patch, no `es8311_dump_registers()` needed. `MIC_GAIN_DB` in
77	`voice/mic.c`.
78	
79	**Rule this cost four builds:** a peak at a repeatable sample index is a
80	transient, not a level problem. Print an 8-segment energy profile before
81	touching gain — `velapaw_mic_stats` does this now.
82	
83	## The other trap: REG44 = 0x50 is ADC-left + DAC-right
84	
85	`es8311_start` sets `ES8311_GPIO_REG44 = 0x50`, so SDOUT carries the mic on
86	the **left** slot and **the DAC's own output on the right**. Patch #25 enabled
87	both RX slots, so playback was being fed straight back into the record stream
88	— a digital feedback loop independent of acoustics. Fixed by patch #28:
89	set `I2S_RX_MONO` (BIT 5 of `I2S_RX_CONF_REG`); `I2S_RX_MONO_FST_VLD` (BIT 9)
90	already defaults to 1 = first slot = the ADC. Keep `TOT_CHAN_NUM=1` (2-slot
91	frame) and both `CHAN_EN` bits — that is the state that moves data.
92	
93	Related: `i2s_rxchannels()` is a no-op and the es8311 driver issues no channel
94	ioctl, so TX TDM stays at its reset default (`txtdm=0x0000ffff`,
95	`TOT_CHAN_NUM=0`) while RX is `0x00010003`. The asymmetry is expected.
96	
97	## Playback loudness is NOT a defect — stop chasing it
98	
99	The amp is on (`board_speaker_enable(true)` runs unconditionally in
100	`board_lcd_initialize`, `g_ioe` assigned 8 lines before, so the NULL
101	early-return can't fire). `DAC_REG32` = `0xC8` = +4.5 dB is the top of the
102	`29*ln(v)` Kconfig mapping. Speech captures at **-24 dBFS average with peaks
103	already at 32767** — a ~24 dB crest factor, which is just what speech is. Any
104	further gain clips those peaks. Only compression raises average without
105	touching peaks, and the ES8311 ALC would pump the noise floor between words,
106	which hurts wake-word detection.
107	
108	Nothing in VelaPaw plays back a live mic: `micro_speech` normalises its own
109	input, and prompts/chimes are full-scale assets ~24 dB louder. **Loopback
110	audibility is not a valid acceptance criterion** — the measured table is.
111	
112	## The "two frozen samples" — DOWNGRADED, probably not a real defect
113	
114	⚠️ **Resolved-ish 2026-08-03: after the cold power cycle that cleared `RX_HUNG`
115	([[velapaw-audio-bringup]]), `dc` no longer pins — it moves freely (-527, -67,
116	0, -6193, +4068, -9511) on the same build 31 binary.** The frozen `dc` was
117	almost certainly an early symptom of the capture path sliding into the hang that
118	followed minutes later, not an independent bug. A buffer holding nothing but two
119	leftover values is what a half-dead RX looks like. Don't spend a build cycle on
120	it unless it reappears on a freshly power-cycled board. The arithmetic below
121	still stands *as arithmetic*; it just no longer describes a live condition.
122	
123	Original finding: `dc` pinned at exactly **-17** over ~100 buffers while `mean`
124	moved freely.
125	`dc = sum/n`, n=2046, so the buffer holds a fixed ~-34,800 = **exactly two
126	samples of -17404**. Confirmed independently: in the quiet tail `mean` bottoms
127	out at exactly 17 = `2*17404/2046`, i.e. those two are the only content left.
128	So it's **two samples, not** the 6-sample 4092/4096 descriptor gap — separate
129	facts; don't conflate them. Matters because a -5.4 dBFS impulse once per
130	128 ms buffer is a 7.8 Hz feature `micro_speech` sees in every frame.
131	
132	Build 32 (md5 `766278060bd24dd980b2b07dca1e4708`) is flashed but its output was
133	never read: meter reports `peak=V@IDX` + last 8 samples as `tail=`. Geometry:
134	`d[0]`=samples 0..2039, `d[1]` starts at 2040, EOF stops at 2045. Repro = one
135	loud clap then ~15 s silence.
136	
137	⚠️ Two traps learned here: (1) the old meter stride `vp_seq & 7` **aliased** —
138	with 4 rotating buffers it always inspected the same `apb` (8 mod 4 == 0); use
139	a stride coprime with 4. (2) `VP: RXDUMP` is emitted from **`i2s_tx_worker`**,
140	one-shot — its position relative to `VP: mic` and its `act/pend/done` counts
141	are scheduling jitter between two workers, **not** state. Don't read meaning
142	into them.
143

Here's what memory has on driving the mic from `nsh`. Flagging up front: these notes are 45–49 days old and the build has moved a long way since (b81+ voice work), so confirm the subcommand names with `velapaw` and no arguments before leaning on them.

**First, you're at `vela>`, not `nsh>`.** The agent CLI owns the console. You need to get back to NSH before any of this works.

## Check audio is actually up

```
ls /dev/audio
```

Must show **`pcm0`** (playback) and **`pcm_in0`** (capture). Both present is the proof the ES8311 init returned OK — nothing else registers those nodes once the `#elif` branch is taken. If `pcm_in0` is missing, the codec didn't come up and nothing below will work.

## Capture from the mic

```
velapaw kws mic 3
```

One session, three captures, prints `peak N@index`, `rms`, `dc`, `rail` and an 8-segment energy profile. Reference numbers at 30 dB gain: silence `rms 26`, a spoken "yes" `rms 645` with the profile loading the back half, "no" `rms 791` loading the front.

## Loopback (speaker ↔ mic)

```
nxlooper
loopback 1 16 16000
q
```

Quit with `q`, not `stop`.

## Three rules that have each cost multiple build cycles

**Only one `velapaw kws mic` per boot.** The second one in the same boot times out at `0/32000` with `-110`, reliably. Only a cold power cycle clears it.

**Never run `velapaw kws mic` before using the voice dialog in the UI.** This is the important one. The CLI task's session teardown wedges the UI worker's session, so the dialog then fails with `rec 0/18 play 1/1 phase -1`. It invalidated two builds' worth of hardware testing while being read as a new bug. If you're demoing voice: cold power cycle, then go *straight* to the feature. The CLI is not a free warm-up.

**A cold power cycle means unplugging USB for ~10 s.** RESET and esptool's RTS reset never drop power to the ES8311, so a latched codec stays latched across both.

## Don't judge it by ear

The mic and speaker are inches apart on the same board, so `loopback` is an acoustic feedback loop — "noisy, can't hear my voice" is what unity loop gain sounds like, and it shifts with any gain change. Read the sample stats, not your ears. Playback being quiet is also not a defect: it's at +4.5 dB, the top of the Kconfig mapping, and speech simply has a ~24 dB crest factor.

What are you trying to do with the mic — demo the voice meal-scheduling dialog, or get audio into the agent?
voice meal scheduling

Here's the protocol. The single most important thing: **do not run `velapaw kws mic` first.** The CLI task's session teardown wedges the UI worker's mic session, and the dialog then fails with `rec 0/18 play 1/1 phase -1`. That misread cost two builds' worth of hardware tests.

## Demo sequence

1. **Unplug USB, wait ~10 s, replug.** A true cold power cycle. RESET and esptool's RTS reset don't drop power to the ES8311, so a latched codec survives both.
2. Enter ×3 for `nsh>`.
3. `ls /dev/audio` — want `pcm0` *and* `pcm_in0`. Thirty seconds, and it tells you whether the codec came up at all.
4. `velapaw` — straight to the app. Nothing else first.
5. **Wait ~30 s before touching voice.** The worker runs unarmed warm-up captures on a delay; the first capture of a boot is the one that decides, and letting it happen while the camera and TFLM model loads are still settling is what made the bad builds bad.
6. My Pets → **Edit** a pet → start the voice dialog.
7. Say the three answers, one word each:
   - **meal**: "one" / "two" / "three"
   - **hour**: "zero" … "nine" (single digit — "eight" gives 08:00)
   - **confirm**: "yes"
8. **Press Save in the modal.** Voice writes the scratch copy deliberately, so it can't bypass Save/Cancel. If you walk away without it, nothing is scheduled.

A good run looks like `heard two 0.773 → heard eight 0.938 → heard yes 0.957 → COMMIT meal 2 = 08:00`, about 9.6 s.

## What not to panic about on stage

- **"Say again" is normal and by design.** The good b68 run had two retries, both correct rejections of bad windows. For a device that commits a feeding schedule, no-false-accept is the property worth having.
- **If you answer the meal step with an hour**, you get `heard "eight" - say 1 / 2 / 3` rather than a bare rejection.
- **Scores swing about 2× between sessions** at what feels like the same volume (0.94–0.96 one session, 0.40–0.76 the next). Speak close to the board and keep the volume consistent.

## The honest caveat

As of the last recorded measurement this was **3 of 5 cold boots**, and a bad boot is bad from its very first capture. The underlying RX stall was never solved — six mechanisms were falsified, and the evidence pointed at the codec's DIN line rather than software. So: cold cycle, try one word, and if it times out, power cycle and go again rather than fighting it. Two tries ≈ 84 %, three ≈ 94 %.

That figure is from build b81 and the tree has moved a long way since, so it may well be better now. Worth running it a few times before the 23rd to get a current number — and if it fails, grab the counters (`velapaw voice`) while the board is still in the failed state, since that's the only thing that distinguishes a real stall from a timing miss.

- **Both models loaded.** `model[0..3]=20 00 00 00` on each — that's a valid TFLite header. If those flash regions had been erased you'd see `ff ff ff ff`, `tflm_init` would return -1 silently, and Recognize would just never match. They're intact, as expected since the flash write stopped at `0x17dfff`.
- **`velapaw/store: history restored from history.bin`** — your feeding history survived too.
- **`mic: 18 buffers x 8192 B`** — the capture session opened with the full deep pool. That's the healthy state.

One thing to keep an eye on: `mic: session belonged to pid 5, reopening`. That's the pid-guard doing its job, but it means something earlier in this boot already owned the mic session — almost certainly `ai_agent`'s `voice_channel_init`, which ran at boot +750 ms. That's structurally the same situation as running `velapaw kws mic` before the dialog, which is the thing that wedges it. **The reopen succeeded**, so you're probably fine — but if the dialog times out, that handover is the first suspect, and the fix is a cold power cycle with `ai_agent` never started.

If it times out, don't retry into it — run `velapaw voice` straight away and paste the counters. `eof N match N miss 0` with a high N means a timing miss; `start 2 busy 2` with `eof 0` means the real stall, and those have completely different answers.

`EXCCAUSE=001c` is 28 — **LoadProhibited**: a read from an address with no read access. On this board that has one dominant cause, and it's documented: a load from PSRAM while the cache PSRAM is reached through has been disabled by a flash/littlefs read.

Look at the ordering in your log. The arena is in PSRAM (`0x3c5d1470`, `0x3c7cff50`), and the last thing before the panic is `history restored from /data/ai_agent/velapaw/history.bin` — a littlefs read. Meanwhile `ai_agent` is still running with `cron` ticking **every 10 seconds** and a heartbeat thread, all of which touch littlefs. That's precisely the mechanism that hard-froze `ask hello` back on 2026-09-02.

So my leading hypothesis is **`velapaw` and `ai_agent` running concurrently**, which they were never designed to do — they're separate builtins and the plan explicitly relied on not needing them at once.

But I'm not going to hand you that as the answer, because **my patch is also a suspect** and I can't rule it out from one line. Two tests, in this order:

**Test A — isolate the concurrency.** Cold power cycle (unplug ~10 s). Enter ×3. Then run **only**:

```
velapaw
```

No `ifconfig`, no `ai_agent`. If it boots clean and the UI is stable, the crash is the concurrency and my patch is exonerated.

**Test B — only if A still panics.** Then it's likely mine, and we have a clean control: the Sept 5 repo image, which I can flash from here in about 30 seconds. Same app, no skip feature.

Either way, **paste me the full panic dump**, not just that line. NuttX prints registers and a backtrace after `xtensa_user_panic` — I need `PC` and especially `EXCVADDR`. If `EXCVADDR` is in `0x3c……`, that's PSRAM and confirms the cache theory outright. If it's near zero, it's a null dereference and a completely different bug.

Also tell me: had you run `velapaw` once already in this boot before this attempt? Two instances fighting over LVGL and the camera would produce something like this too, and the `session belonged to pid 5` line says *something* had already claimed the mic.
after reboot the ui is alright but once i run velapaw the ui freezes without running the agent or is the agent auto running?

That reframes it completely — and it fits `pid 5`.

A pid that low means the task started at boot from the init script, not from anything you typed. So **VelaPaw is almost certainly already running when you reach `nsh>`** — that's the UI you see and describe as "alright". Typing `velapaw` then starts a *second* instance, which re-initialises LVGL, re-allocates the 768 KB PSRAM arena, re-opens the camera and takes the mic session off the first instance (`session belonged to pid 5, reopening`). Instance one is left holding pointers into memory instance two just reallocated — and a load through one of those is exactly `EXCCAUSE=001c`.

So: **the UI freezing when you run `velapaw` is you launching a duplicate.** Not the agent, and — tentatively — not my patch.

To confirm, reboot and at `nsh>` run this **before** typing anything else:

```
ps
```

That answers both your questions at once. If there's a `velapaw` task already in the list, that's your UI and you should never launch it again. If `ai_agent` is also there, it's auto-starting too; if it isn't, it only ran earlier because you typed `ai_agent &`.

Paste the `ps` output.

Which also means my earlier instructions were wrong on that point — I had you launching a second copy. Sorry about that; `ps` will settle it.

Checked — that requirement is **obsolete, and it isn't your problem anyway.**

It was real: the board used to need a PC draining COM4, because `es8311.c` carries 32 `auderr` calls (one inside the driver's audio worker loop) and with nothing reading the port, the 193-byte CDCACM TX buffer filled and the syslog write blocked the thread doing capture. But it was fixed in **b83** by turning `CONFIG_DEBUG_AUDIO_ERROR` and `_WARN` off — confirmed with one cold cycle and five RESETs, no terminal, mic working. Raising the buffer size was tried at 2048 and is explicitly *not* the fix. And you have PuTTY open right now, so even the old behaviour wouldn't bite.

"Listening but not responding" is the other, unsolved one: the first capture of a boot intermittently stalls, and a bad boot is bad from its very first capture. Historically 3 of 5 cold boots.

Get the counters **while it's still in the failed state** — this is the only moment they mean anything:

```
velapaw voice
```

That's a probe subcommand: it reads the running instance's statics and exits, so it won't start a second UI the way bare `velapaw` did. Paste everything it prints.

What I'm looking for:

- `i2s eof N match N miss 0` with a **high N** → the mic is fine and the dialog's patience ran out. Tunable.
- `eof 0 ... start 2 busy 2`, `desc 80000ff0`, `intraw 000000a0` → the real RX stall. The DMA is armed and no samples are arriving from the codec. Nothing in software fixes that one — six mechanisms were falsified against it — and the answer is a **cold power cycle: unplug USB ~10 s, replug.** RESET doesn't clear it, because neither RESET nor RTS drops power to the ES8311.

If it is the stall, don't retry into it. Power cycle and go straight to My Pets → Edit without touching anything else first.
what is the command

At the `nsh>` prompt:

```
velapaw voice
```

If it comes back "unknown", try:

```
velapaw help
```

Don't run `velapaw` with no arguments — that's the one that starts a second UI and freezes the board.

velapaw voice
velapaw/voice probe: init_rc 0  loops 1872  caps 2  lastret -110
velapaw/voice probe: run 0  ready 0  fail 0  evt 0  dismissed 0
velapaw/voice probe: preopen 0  capms 3500  dialogms 8000

velapaw/voice probe: i2s isr 0 noeof 0 last 00000000  act 1 pend 1 done 0
velapaw/voice probe: i2s desc 80000ff0 80000010 00000000 00000000
velapaw/voice probe: i2s intraw 000000a0 intena 00000002 inlink 001ab284
velapaw/voice probe: i2s cfgskip 0 chst 11 resc 2 kick 2
velapaw/voice probe: recover mickick 2 ok 0  capfail 2 consec 2
velapaw/voice probe: mic open0 pid 5 seq 1  reccfg 1 recstart 5 playstart 5  bufs 18  ret 0
velapaw/voice probe: mic fail got 0/32000  seq 0  phase -1
velapaw/voice probe: mic fail rec 0/36  play 2/2 (tail/head)
velapaw/voice probe: vsched state 0  slot 0  hour 0  tries 0
velapaw/voice log: 5 events, oldest first:
   45080 === dialog start ===
   45080 -> step1 (slot 0 hour 0)
   52620 cap FAILED -110 (1 in a row)
   53110 mic never became ready in 8000ms
   60350 cap FAILED -110 (2 in a row)
nsh>

That's the real RX stall, not a timing miss. The signature is exact and matches the recorded invariant from builds b76–b80 line for line:

```
i2s eof 0 match 0 miss 0 empty 0   start 3 busy 1
i2s desc 80000ff0 80000010          owner bit set, length 0
i2s intraw 000000a0 intena 00000002 IN_SUC_EOF enabled, never fires
mic fail rec 0/36  play 2/2
```

RX accepted 36 buffers and returned **none**. TX completed 2 of 2 through the same GDMA block, same clock, same peripheral — so the clock is running and the EOF path works. The descriptor's owner bit is set with zero bytes written: **the DMA is armed and no samples are arriving from the codec.** `intraw 000000a0` is INFIFO_FULL_WM + INFIFO_UDF_L1 re-asserting after each kick, which is live starvation, not stale state. And `mickick 2 ok 0` — the recovery kick provably ran and cleared nothing.

Nothing in software fixes this. Six mechanisms were falsified against it with hardware counters, and the evidence points below the DMA, at the ES8311 ADC path.

**Stop testing this boot, right now.** `capfail 2 consec 2` — the budget is 3. One more attempt latches `g_voice_fail`, the worker thread exits, and voice is dead until reboot.

**Unplug the USB cable, wait ~10 seconds, plug it back in.** Not RESET — neither RESET nor esptool's RTS drops power to the ES8311, so a latched codec survives both. Only removing power clears it.

Then, in this order and nothing else:
1. Wait ~30 s after boot.
2. Go straight to My Pets → Edit → dialog on the UI that's already running.
3. Don't type `velapaw`, don't start `ai_agent`, don't run `velapaw kws mic`.

Historically this is about 3 boots in 5, so budget for repeats — two tries ≈ 84 %, three ≈ 94 %.

For the 23rd, plan the demo around it rather than hoping: power cycle immediately before the voice segment, and have the meal-skip tap and the `ask` flow ready as the segments that always work. If you want, after the 23rd we can put the logic analyzer on GPIO14 + BCLK + WS during a stalled capture — DIN flat while the clocks toggle would finally pin this to the codec side rather than the SoC.

2. **Key Technical Concepts**

   - **Unified-diff patch validation by round-trip**: reverse-apply to post-state, forward-apply, `diff -q` for byte identity. `patch -l` needed because two hunks contain blank context lines (single trailing space at patch lines 28 and 32).
   - **`grep -c` counts lines, not occurrences** — 8 not 9 for `g_meal_skipped` because `g_meal_skipped[pet][slot] = !g_meal_skipped[pet][slot];` holds two references on one line.
   - **Binary string forensics**: `[Text.Encoding]::GetEncoding(28591)` (byte-preserving; `Latin1` doesn't exist in .NET Framework 4.x) to test for i18n literals in `nuttx.bin`. Comparing *all* ~70 English strings isolates the one missing source change; checking a single string proves nothing.

Fifteen of them: thirteen counters plus two functions, `velapaw_i2s_rxdbg` and `velapaw_i2s_rxdesc`, called from [ui_lvgl.c:3269](apps/examples/velapaw/ui/ui_lvgl.c#L3269) and [ui_lvgl.c:3302](apps/examples/velapaw/ui/ui_lvgl.c#L3302).

Worth flagging separately, because it outlives tonight's experiment: the first build didn't recompile even though the `.c` was newer than the `.o`. It only rebuilt once `staging/libarch.a` was deleted. That means the top level was treating `libarch.a` as satisfied regardless of arch sources — so **any** edit under `arch/` has been silently dropped from builds, for an unknown span. The Sept 3 timestamp is the floor on how long, not necessarily the start. That's worth recording once we're through here.

356	WS 15, MCLK 12, DOUT 16 — and `esp32s3_st7789.c:411` independently warns that
357	IO12–16 are the codec's I2S bus). Next moves are hardware, not software:
358	bisect what changed physically since the last good b83 boot, then put the FX2
359	logic analyzer on GPIO14 + BCLK + WS during a capture. DIN flat while BCLK/WS
360	toggle ⇒ codec/mic side; DIN toggling ⇒ SoC pad/mux side.
